1	// What a policy covers, and what it pays out. The mirror image of pricing.ts:
2	// that module answers what the customer pays us, this one answers what we pay
3	// the customer. Both are asked by claim-office.ts, which knows the order the
4	// questions come in; neither knows anything about scenarios or steps.
5	
6	import { type Item, type KnownItemType } from "./pricing.js";
7	
8	export interface Damage {
9	  itemType: string;
10	  amount: number;
11	}
12	
13	// What an item is insured FOR, as opposed to what insuring it costs. Payout
14	// caps are derived from these; premiums are not.
15	const INSURANCE_VALUE_BY_TYPE: Record<KnownItemType, number> = {
16	  sword: 1000,
17	  amulet: 600,
18	  staff: 800,
19	  potion: 400,
20	  rune: 250,
21	  moonstone: 250,
22	};
23	
24	const insuranceSumOf = (items: Item[]): number =>
25	  items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + INSURANCE_VALUE_BY_TYPE[item.type], 0);
26	
27	const CAP_MULTIPLE_OF_INSURANCE_SUM = 2;
28	
29	// A policy pays out at most twice what its items are insured for. Premium
30	// modifiers — curses, enchantments, block discounts — shift what the policy
31	// COSTS and never what it COVERS, so the cap reads insurance values only.
32	export const capFor = (items: Item[]): number =>
33	  CAP_MULTIPLE_OF_INSURANCE_SUM * insuranceSumOf(items);
34	
35	// What a claim actually pays, once the policy's own limit is consulted. The
36	// cap is a running total: a policy pays out at most twice its insurance sum
37	// ACROSS all its claims, so each settlement both reads the cap left to it and
38	// reports what remains for the next one.
39	//
40	// Lives here beside capFor rather than in the orchestrator: establishing the
41	// limit and enforcing it are one rule, and claim-office.ts is only meant to
42	// know the order the questions come in, not the answers.
43	export interface Settlement {
44	  payout: number;
45	  remainingCap: number;
46	}
47	
48	export const settleClaim = (
49	  grossPayout: number,
50	  remainingCap: number,
51	): Settlement => {
52	  const payout = Math.min(grossPayout, remainingCap);
53	  return { payout, remainingCap: remainingCap - payout };
54	};
55	
56	const DEDUCTIBLE_PER_DAMAGE = 100;
57	
58	const HALF_REIMBURSEMENT_ENCHANTMENT_THRESHOLD = 8;
59	const HALF_REIMBURSEMENT_SHARE = 0.5;
60	
61	const FULL_REIMBURSEMENT_SHARE = 1;
62	
63	// Named for the clause it gates rather than for a degree of enchantment:
64	// pricing.ts has its own, LOWER enchantment threshold (>= 5, a premium
65	// surcharge), and the two are easy to confuse when both read as adjectives.
66	const qualifiesForHalfReimbursement = (item: Item): boolean =>
67	  (item.enchantment ?? 0) >= HALF_REIMBURSEMENT_ENCHANTMENT_THRESHOLD;
68	
69	// The reimbursement clauses in the order the MHPCO applies them: the FIRST
70	// matching clause decides the share, later ones never override it. Order is
71	// the whole content of the rule, so the list is written out even though the
72	// dragon clause and the default agree — see the note below.
73	//
74	// Half reimbursement: the MHPCO holds that a strongly enchanted item's magic
75	// bears part of its own misfortune.
76	const REIMBURSEMENT_CLAUSES: {
77	  applies: (item: Item) => boolean;
78	  share: number;
79	}[] = [
80	  { applies: qualifiesForHalfReimbursement, share: HALF_REIMBURSEMENT_SHARE },
81	  { applies: () => true, share: FULL_REIMBURSEMENT_SHARE },
82	];
83	
84	// Deliberately ABSENT: the spec's "dragon material => full reimbursement"
85	// clause, which would sit above the half clause. It is unwritten because it is
86	// untestable from the spec's examples — full reimbursement is also the default,
87	// so every dragon example yields the same payout with or without it. The one
88	// case that WOULD distinguish the two orderings, a dragon item with
89	// enchantment >= 8, is fixed by example at HALF (see the enchantment-9 test),
90	// which is the opposite of what a dragon-first clause would pay. So the spec's
91	// own examples contradict placing a dragon clause first, and no example
92	// justifies placing it anywhere else. Adding one here would be guesswork
93	// dressed as fidelity; `material` stays unread until an example forces it.
94	
95	const reimbursementShareFor = (item: Item): number =>
96	  REIMBURSEMENT_CLAUSES.find(({ applies }) => applies(item))?.share ??
97	  FULL_REIMBURSEMENT_SHARE;
98	
99	const reimbursementFor = (item: Item, damage: Damage): number =>
100	  damage.amount * reimbursementShareFor(item);
101	
102	// The customer bears the first 100 G of each damage entry separately, so two
103	// damaged swords carry two deductibles rather than one. The deductible comes
104	// off AFTER the reimbursement clauses have reduced the amount.
105	//
106	// Named for the single subtraction it performs, not for the final payout: this
107	// result is neither floored at zero nor limited by the policy's remaining cap.
108	// Both of those are still it.todo() in the spec ("exhausts the cap across
109	// successive claims", "rejects a claim containing a damage entry with a
110	// negative amount") and will be forced by those tests. Until then the name
111	// must not claim a settlement it does not compute.
112	const netOfDeductible = (item: Item, damage: Damage): number =>
113	  reimbursementFor(item, damage) - DEDUCTIBLE_PER_DAMAGE;
114	
115	// Which insured item a damage entry is about. A damage names its item by type,
116	// so the first item of that type answers it. That is exact while a policy
117	// holds at most one item per type; the test rejecting more damage entries of a
118	// type than the policy covers is what will force a real pairing.
119	const damagedItem = (items: Item[], damage: Damage): Item | undefined =>
120	  items.find((item) => item.type === damage.itemType);
121	
122	export const payoutForDamages = (items: Item[], damages: Damage[]): number =>
123	  damages.reduce((total, damage) => {
124	    const item = damagedItem(items, damage);
125	    return total + (item === undefined ? 0 : netOfDeductible(item, damage));
126	  }, 0);

Baseline: 31 passing, tsc clean.

**Step 1: Naming Evaluation (first priority).**

Working through the recently-touched surface in `coverage.ts`:

- `payoutForDamages(items, damages)` — reveals intent, and correctly does *not* claim to be a settlement. Keep.
- `netOfDeductible` — the file's own comment argues carefully for this name. Keep.
- `damagedItem(items, damage)` — this is the one. The name asserts it returns *the* damaged item, but the body returns the first item merely *matching the damage's type*. The name is a promise the function does not keep, and the incoming test ("more damage entries of a type than the policy covers") is precisely the case where the promise breaks. **Rename to `firstItemOfDamagedType`.**

**Step 2: APP mass, before.**

`damagedItem` + the `payoutForDamages` reducer:

```
damagedItem: bindings items,damage,item = 3; invocations find,(===) = 2×2 = 4  → 7
payoutForDamages: bindings items,damages,total,damage,item = 5;
  invocations damagedItem,reduce,(+),(+) = 4×2 = 8;
  constants 0, undefined = 2;
  conditionals ternary = 4;
  invocation netOfDeductible = 2                                              → 21
Subtotal: 28
```

**Step 3: Simple Design rules.**

- Rule 1 (tests pass): green. ✅
- Rule 2 (reveals intent): the `damagedItem` name misreports. This is the improvement.
- Rule 3 (duplication): none found — `pricing.ts` and `coverage.ts` both hold a clause-list-with-`applies` shape, but they are *conceptually* different rules (premium surcharges that stack additively vs. reimbursement clauses where first-match wins). Unifying them would be incidental-duplication removal that hurts clarity. Rule 2 trumps Rule 3 here. Skip.
- Rule 4 (fewest elements): resisted the temptation to inline `damagedItem` into the reducer. It is the exact seam the next test must widen, and inlining would obscure that.

**Step 4: Implement — one change.**

content.text:
31 passing, tsc clean.

**Step 5: APP mass, after.** 28 → 28 (Δ 0). Pure rename: no component added or removed. Rule 2 improvement with no mass cost.

**Step 6/7: Refactoring report.**

🔄 Refactoring Complete
- **Refactoring**: renamed `damagedItem` → `firstItemOfDamagedType` in `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-08-10_19-39-03_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.6-lab-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking/src/coverage.ts`, and rewrote its comment to state the actual defect the simplification hides.
- **Mass Change**: 28 → 28 (Δ 0)
- **Tests**: 31 passing ✅, `tsc --noEmit` clean ✅

Why this one, over the alternatives:

The old name was the only place in the tree where an identifier asserted something the code does not do. `damagedItem` reads as "the item this damage is about"; the body returns the first item whose type matches. Those coincide only while a policy holds at most one item per type. Under Rule 2 a name that misreports is worse than a verbose one that is true, so the honest name wins even though it is longer.

Rejected deliberately:

- **Rule 3 (duplication)**: `pricing.ts`'s `ITEM_SURCHARGES` and `coverage.ts`'s `REIMBURSEMENT_CLAUSES` share a `{ applies, rate|share }[]` shape, but their semantics are opposites — surcharges `filter` and sum additively, reimbursement clauses `find` first-match-wins. A shared abstraction would unify the syntax of two rules that differ in exactly the way that matters. Incidental, not real, duplication.
- **Rule 4 (fewest elements)**: inlining the helper into the `payoutForDamages` reducer would shed one binding, but it is the precise seam the next test must widen. Keeping it named leaves the change local.

One thing worth flagging for the next cycle, found while reading rather than introduced:

Your prompt framed the two-identical-swords pass as indistinguishable from proper pairing. That is right for the payout, but the first-match simplification is already a *latent overpayment*, not merely an under-specification. Two damage entries of type `sword` against a policy holding one sword currently both resolve to that same sword and pay out twice — bounded only by `remainingCap`, which is why no existing example catches it. So the upcoming test is not adding a new rule so much as exposing a live bug. The fix is the same either way: `payoutForDamages` becomes a fold carrying the not-yet-consumed items, each insured item matched at most once, with the leftover damages driving the rejection path. `firstItemOfDamagedType`'s `undefined` branch — currently contributing 0 — is where that error will naturally originate.
